extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural designers, craftsmen, and students of architectural ornament
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principles for designing and arranging architectural ornament so it is appropriate to execution, visible at intended distances, and unified by hierarchy and law. Covers practical constraints of craftsmanship, visual adaptation to distance, and moral/aesthetic principles of subordination and unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for cooperative execution by inferior workmen
rubrics_metrics.description: Your business as an architect is to calculate only on the co-operation of inferior men, to think for them, and to indicate for them such expressions of your thoughts as the weakest capacity can comprehend and the feeblest hand can execute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architectural ornament should be conceived so it can be executed by large numbers of less-skilled workmen; do not demand that every ornamental detail be wrought by great artists. Examples: Giotto may design but cannot carve all; a great designer must map out lines so two thousand men can work upon them with confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not require all ornament to be executed in a 'great' manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid fastidiousness in execution that diminishes the possible number and grandeur of buildings — greatness is not available in the required quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insisting that every part be executed by 'thoughtful men' reduces the scale and frequency of architectural works. Expect practical limitations in the supply of highly skilled artisans; design to fit available labour rather than attempt to educate a workforce to an impractical standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and employ individual value of lesser minds (medieval ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The glory of Gothic architecture is that every jot and tittle affords room, fuel, and focus for individual fire; the mediseval system recognises the mind of the inferior workman and gives him full room for action guided by a ruling mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a leading/ruling designer who ennobles and guides many individual hands rather than attempting total servility of execution. This system allows many contributors to add vitality even if they lack learned 'science.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt ornament to the distance of the eye
rubrics_metrics.description: The ornament must be calculated for a given viewing distance; delicate finish appropriate at close range is useless or even harmful at great distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not carve near-level detail for elements meant to be seen from forty feet; delicate work can be worse at distance than rough work. Observe that painting and nature have particular distances for which their effects are produced; architecture must do the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two modes of distance-adaptation: crude reduction vs redesigned simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: First mode: same designs are rudely cut with fewer details when remote. Second mode (higher): adopt a different design composed of fewer parts and simpler lines cut with exquisite precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The second method is the superior and more intentional one; the first may be confounded with mere economy or slovenliness. Both produce imperfection when seen close, but the second yields a deliberate, satisfactory adaptation for distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplification for distance
rubrics_metrics.description: One branch of adapting design for distance: simplify the design so fewer delicate passages remain and the prominent features read clearly from afar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject delicate passages that vanish at distance; fix thought on arranging features that will remain visible far away. Simplification can preserve a sense of delicacy even in bolder markings by choosing forms that hold up at the intended distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis (linear method/Proutism) for distance
rubrics_metrics.description: The other branch of adaptation is emphasis — using explanatory lines, deep incisions, and linear drawing to make subjects intelligible at distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deep narrow incisions can create black lines on stone visible in sunshine like chalk on paper; patterns and armor details may be simply incised rather than carved in relief to be legible. Samuel Prout's drawings and the Romans' practice of outlining small reliefs are cited as models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament's excellence depends on fitting a particular distance
rubrics_metrics.description: The excellence of an ornament depends upon its fitting its intended viewing distance, being seen better there than anywhere else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design so the spectator is satisfied to remain where he is, feeling the decoration equally rich from its intended vantage; e.g., some capitals appear richest from below and less delicate when approached — that is correct if intended for that distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple hierarchical (arborescent) orders adapted to different distances
rubrics_metrics.description: Good ornamentation is arborescent: lesser ornaments are grafted on greater ones in successive orders, each adapted for a different distance (great masses for far, traceries for nearer, niches/statues for close).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan ornament in layers: large masses to define form at miles, traceries and shafts for approach, niches and robes for standing beneath. Each order should be subordinate to a greater, simpler, and more powerful one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination of parts within orders; avoid competing elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever order of ornament is contemplated, its parts must be subordinated to a greater order; if figurings, chasings, and borderings are not subordinated to folds, and folds to mass, and mass to the building, then the ornament is bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid elements vying for attention simultaneously; maintain clear hierarchy so each element supports a larger structural or visual whole. Lack of subordination is an error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept inevitable intermediate viewing distances and bold separation between orders
rubrics_metrics.description: There cannot be orders adapted to every distance; between ranks there will be intermediate distances where viewers feel ill-placed and wish to move nearer or farther.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design acknowledges and accepts such dissatisfied vantage points as natural; do not attempt impossible uniform legibility across all distances — use bold separation between orders instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid democratic ornament (equal emphasis everywhere)
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic ornament, in which all elements are equally influential and contest for attention, is visually poor and leads to uninteresting, invisible details at distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The English perpendicular is cited as an example: covering walls with equal reticulation and equal foils produces invisible or uninteresting detail. Prefer division into large masses with minute surface work that fills but does not break the masses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement and method before quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: First consider the method of arranging ornament; the advisable quantity of ornament depends upon the method and should be decided after method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply ornament by indiscriminate abundance; determine the method (how ornament will express laws and hierarchy) and then decide how much ornament is wise in that system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience to external law: ornament must willingly submit to limits
rubrics_metrics.description: One necessity of good ornament is the acknowledgment and willing submission of the ornament to an enclosing fitness or limit — not forcing nature into a cage, but having the 'spirit' of the law within the ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The value is not mere confinement but that the ornament anticipates and accepts the limitation as natural; the spirit of the formal law must be put into the motif so that elements grow with 'a sense of triangular necessity' rather than being clipped into shape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate, justified transgression of law as accent
rubrics_metrics.description: A slight breaking of the prevailing law or limit in ornament can heighten expression if presented as a special, chosen infringement (like a miracle permitted by a higher need).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: small beasts laying paws across an enclosing fillet; such exceptions should be conscious, mutually consented, and feel like a granted permission rather than an accidental lapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal headship and alternation of light and shade as a source of unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Obedience to an internal headship (unity) and the alternation of shade with light (continuous ornament like dentils and billet mouldings) form chief elements of ornament's charm and unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This alternation typifies deeper oppositions (e.g., labor/rest, life/death) and provides a visual chain that the eye never wearies of. It is both an expression of divine law and a physical fact essential to continuous ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design to prevent accidental shadows from concealing expression
rubrics_metrics.description: When ornament is placed at a distance, details should be marked so accidental shadows cannot conceal or alter expression (e.g., sharp thin lips and drilled holes in the iris for distant sculpture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear, strong lines and features in distant work to ensure legibility under varying light; the example of the Adam head at the Ducal Palace shows choices made so features read correctly from below.
